scenario: A 67-year-old male admitted for community-acquired pneumonia is found confused and bradycardic after a potassium replacement medication error. The case focuses on recognition and treatment of hyperkalemic emergency with unstable bradycardia and possible progression to ventricular fibrillation arrest.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Atropine 0.5 mg IV push now, symptomatic bradycardia. HR's 40 with BP 90/50 and he's a bit altered. Set up for a repeat dose and get the pads on in case we need to pace.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Your heart's beating too slowly, so I'm getting a heart tracing right now. Tell me what you're feeling and when it started, and are you on any pills for your heart or blood pressure?

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: Your heart's beating too slowly, so I'm getting a heart tracing right now. Tell me what you're feeling and when it started, and are you on any pills for your heart or blood pressure?] fear absent->present: the clinician directly discloses to the symptomatic/unstable patient that his heart is beating dangerously slowly and is getting an urgent tracing - a serious clinical threat that raises fear at least to present; the questions sustain rather than soothe. sadness stays absent: no disclosure of loss or devastating outcome. overwhelm stays absent: a single finding plus a couple of straightforward questions, not a pile of complex information exceeding capacity. shame stays absent: no blame, judgment, or exposure.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: I just feel awful... all muddled up, can't think straight. I've got high blood pressure, I take ramipril and that water pill, the HCTZ. What's wrong with me?

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Send a basic metabolic panel now. I want potassium and renal function given he's on HCTZ and this bradycardia.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: ECG's back — peaked T waves. BMP is sent, potassium and renal pending, ready in a couple minutes. Heads up, his rhythm's dropped to sinus brady at 32 and pressure's down to 73/40 now, worse than at your last look. Pads are on, atropine's in and a repeat's drawn up.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Start transcutaneous pacing now. He's refractory to atropine, HR 32, BP 73/40 and altered.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Pacer pads on, transcutaneous pacing initiated. I'll titrate output and confirm electrical and mechanical capture.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: BMP's back — potassium 8.2, that's your cause. Na 138, Cl 107, HCO3 24, Cr 108, glucose 5.6. Pacing's captured, HR 45, BP 75/42, sats 99%. Want calcium gluconate and insulin-dextrose ready?

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Give calcium gluconate IV now — potassium's 8.2 with peaked Ts, we need cardiac membrane stabilization first.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Calcium gluconate is in.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Calcium's in for stabilization. Now give insulin with dextrose IV to shift the potassium down — K's 8.2, that's the next step.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Insulin and dextrose are in for the hyperkalemia. I'll recheck the glucose in 30 minutes and monitor for hypoglycemia.

available_results.name: Basic Metabolic Panel
available_results.result: Na 138, K 8.2, Cl 107, HCO3 24, Urea 5.5, Cr 108, Glucose 5.6

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Give sodium bicarbonate IV now. Calcium and insulin-dextrose only shift the potassium temporarily — K's still 8.2 and we need to actually bring the total-body potassium down.

available_results.name: Basic Metabolic Panel
available_results.result: Na 138, K 8.2, Cl 107, HCO3 24, Urea 5.5, Cr 108, Glucose 5.6

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Get me a repeat ECG now — I want to see those peaked T waves resolving after the calcium and insulin-dextrose.

available_results.name: Basic Metabolic Panel
available_results.result: Na 138, K 8.2, Cl 107, HCO3 24, Urea 5.5, Cr 108, Glucose 5.6

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Your heart rhythm and blood pressure have improved with the treatments we've given. I need to know what caused this — do you have kidney problems or take any regular medications, and have you missed any doses recently?

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Repeat ECG's back — it's showing a sine-wave pattern. That's worsening, not resolving. Current rhythm's sinus at 66, BP 90/50, sats 99%.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: Kidneys? I don't know about any of that. It's just the ramipril and that water pill for my blood pressure, like I told you. And don't ask me about missed doses — I'm all muddled up, I can't even think straight, never mind remember. I still feel awful.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Repeat calcium gluconate IV now — the repeat ECG's a sine-wave pattern, that's a peri-arrest sign. This is a deliberate second dose for membrane stabilization.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Calcium gluconate is in and running. I'll keep him on continuous cardiac monitoring.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Nebulized salbutamol now as an additional shifting agent — K's still 8.2 with a sine-wave ECG despite calcium, insulin-dextrose and bicarb. And get renal on the phone; with his ramipril and diuretic he'll need dialysis for definitive potassium removal.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: I'm putting you on a nebulizer with salbutamol now to help bring your potassium down. You may feel your heart race or a bit shaky — that's expected. Breathe it in steadily for me.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: I need to be straight with you. The potassium in your blood is dangerously high, at 8.2, and that's what's throwing off your heart's rhythm. The medicines we've given so far only buy us time — they don't actually remove the potassium. To clear it, you'll need dialysis. Your ramipril and that water pill for your blood pressure very likely let the potassium build up to this level.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: Dialysis? God... I heard you, the potassium's too high. But I still feel awful, all muddled up, I can't think straight. Do I really need that?

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Yes, you really do need it. The medicines we've given only shift the potassium out of the way for a while — they wear off, and none of them remove it from your blood. Dialysis is the only thing that actually pulls it out. That high potassium, at 8.2, is exactly why you feel muddled and can't think straight, and it's what's affecting your heart. So dialysis isn't optional here.
